prompt: Some people believe that governments should place a heavy tax on foods that are high in sugar and fat in order to improve public health. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
essay:
Behind this question sits an assumption worth examining: that the problem is what people choose, and that a tax works by making them choose differently. Read that way the levy is a blunt instrument, mildly punitive and easy to resent. I support it, but for a reason that has very little to do with the shopper at the checkout.

Diets did not deteriorate because whole populations lost their willpower simultaneously. They deteriorated because the cheapest, most available and most heavily marketed calories were reformulated over half a century to be as close to irresistible as food engineering could make them. Asking individuals to out-compete that through discipline alone is a strategy with an unbroken record of failure, and the moralising that accompanies it does real damage to the people it targets.

A tax banded by composition changes the incentive at the point where the decisions are actually taken. A manufacturer facing a threshold will quietly take sugar out of a recipe rather than surrender a price advantage, and consumers who never read a label and never intended to change anything consume less sugar. That is the entire case, and it is a strong one: it operates on the environment rather than the individual, so it requires nobody to be persuaded of anything.

Two conditions follow. The levy has to be graded rather than flat, since a flat charge gives no reason to reformulate and merely raises the price of an unchanged product. And it has to be paired with supply — fresh food that is genuinely cheaper and genuinely nearby — or it becomes a charge on people whose alternatives are theoretical. Without both, the criticism that it punishes poverty is not a smear; it is accurate.

So I agree with the proposal, with the caveat that its purpose is routinely misdescribed. Taxes of this sort do not work by shaming. They work by making the reformulated version the commercially obvious one, which is why the healthiest possible outcome is a tax that eventually collects almost nothing.
title: Taxing sugar and fat
